cards.front: What is the most common factor among all collisions in Indiana?
cards.back: Failure to yield the right of way is the most common factor among all collisions in Indiana.

cards.front: What often causes crashes?
cards.back: Crashes are often caused by a driver's inattention, failure to follow the rules of the road, or both.

cards.front: What must a driver involved in a crash do first?
cards.back: A driver involved in a crash must stop immediately, or as close to the scene as possible without blocking traffic more than necessary.

cards.front: When must a driver move a crashed vehicle off the highway, and when not?
cards.back: If the crash happens on the traveled part of a highway, the driver must move the vehicle off the highway near the scene, unless the crash involves hazardous materials or causes injury, death or entrapment.

cards.front: When does a crashed vehicle stay where it is instead of being moved off the road?
cards.back: A crash on the traveled highway is normally moved off the road, but a crash with hazardous materials, injury, death or entrapment stays where it is.

cards.front: What must a driver give and show at a crash scene?
cards.back: A driver must stay at the crash scene, give their name, address and vehicle registration number to everyone involved, and show their driver's license.

cards.front: What must a driver do when a crash injures or kills someone?
cards.back: When a crash injures or kills someone, the driver must give reasonable help to people hurt or trapped as directed by police, medical staff or a nine one one operator, and should make sure police are notified as soon as possible.

cards.front: What should you do after hitting an unattended vehicle or other property?
cards.back: After hitting an unattended vehicle or other property, stop, stay at the scene, try to notify the owner, and call police with the information if the owner cannot be found.

cards.front: What must your insurer file after a crash if the BMV asks?
cards.back: After a crash, if the BMV asks, your insurer must electronically file a Certificate of Compliance showing you had at least the state minimum liability coverage at the time.

cards.front: What are the three ways to avoid a collision?
cards.back: To avoid a collision you can stop quickly, turn quickly away from the danger if you cannot stop in time, or speed up when accelerating is the best or only way out.

cards.front: If a crash looks likely, which way should you steer, and how should you leave the road?
cards.back: If a crash looks likely, steer away from oncoming traffic even if that means leaving the road, and drive off the road rather than skidding off.

cards.front: If you must hit something, what should you choose?
cards.back: If you must hit something, pick something that gives way, like brush, over something hard, and a vehicle moving your way over a still object, but a still object is safer than a head-on crash.

cards.front: How do the possible impacts rank from best to worst?
cards.back: Hitting something moving your way beats hitting something standing still, but hitting something standing still beats a head-on crash, and a sideswipe can help you slow down.

cards.front: What should you do if your wheels drift onto the shoulder?
cards.back: If your wheels drift onto the shoulder, do not jerk back onto the pavement; drive along the shoulder, ease off the gas and steer back gradually after slowing.

cards.front: What can happen if you pull back onto the pavement too quickly?
cards.back: Pulling back onto the pavement too quickly after drifting onto the shoulder can throw the vehicle off balance.

cards.front: How long does a car that plunges into water usually float?
cards.back: A car that plunges into water usually floats for several minutes, giving occupants time to escape through an open window while it is still on the surface.

cards.front: Should you try to open a door in a car that is in water?
cards.back: In a car in water, do not try to open a door, because water pressure makes it nearly impossible and an open door floods the inside.

cards.front: What are the steps to escape a car in water?
cards.back: In a car in water, remove your seat belt, open a window, free children from restraints, climb out onto the roof and call nine one one, and never go back in for belongings.

cards.front: Do power windows usually work after a car goes into water?
cards.back: Power windows usually still open after a car enters water unless the impact damaged the electrical system.

cards.front: How should passengers be helped in a car in water?
cards.back: In a car in water, have older children help younger ones and move passengers to the front seats as calmly as possible.

cards.front: Why ride on the roof of a car in water, and when do you swim?
cards.back: Riding on the roof of a car in water keeps you as dry as possible, and swimming for shore is a last resort if help has not come before the car sinks.

cards.front: How does alcohol affect a driver, and what sets blood alcohol concentration?
cards.back: Alcohol harms clear thinking and physical coordination and slows reaction time, and blood alcohol concentration depends mainly on how much is drunk, how fast and the person's body weight.

cards.front: What should you do before driving if you take a medicine?
cards.back: Many prescription, over-the-counter and recreational drugs impair reasoning and coordination, so check the label and ask a physician or pharmacist about side effects before driving.

cards.front: What are some signs of a possibly impaired driver?
cards.back: Signs of a possibly impaired driver include wide turns, straddling the center line or weaving, unusual speed, near misses, stopping for no reason, and driving at night without headlights.

cards.front: What other warning signs point to an impaired driver?
cards.back: Other warning signs of an impaired driver include swerving or drifting, following too closely, abrupt or illegal turns and inconsistent signaling.

cards.front: What should you do first in a roadside emergency?
cards.back: In a roadside emergency, pull onto the shoulder if you can and turn on your hazard lights.

cards.front: Where should you place a red emergency reflective triangle?
cards.back: Place a red emergency reflective triangle two hundred feet behind your vehicle, or five hundred feet behind it on a hill or curve.

cards.front: How should you get out of a car on a roadside shoulder?
cards.back: If you have to get out on a roadside shoulder, exit on the passenger side after checking for traffic, obstructions and drop-offs.

cards.front: Are the manual's roadside emergency tips required by law?
cards.back: The manual's roadside emergency tips are safety guidelines that are not necessarily required by Indiana law.

cards.front: What should you keep in the vehicle for roadside emergencies?
cards.back: Keep a flashlight with fresh batteries within the driver's reach, plus a reflective safety vest and a red reflective triangle in the vehicle.

cards.front: What winter supplies should you pack?
cards.back: In winter, pack blankets, extra gloves and warm hats in case you must wait for responders or a tow.

cards.front: What should you do in a tire blowout?
cards.back: In a blowout, hold the wheel firmly, keep going straight, take your foot off the gas without braking, and brake only when the car is almost stopped off the road.

cards.front: What should you do if conventional brakes fail?
cards.back: If conventional brakes fail, move to a lower gear when you can, then press the brake pedal hard and fast a few times to build up pressure.

cards.front: How does braking differ between a blowout and a brake failure?
cards.back: In a blowout you avoid the brakes until the car is nearly stopped, while in brake failure you pump the pedal hard to build pressure.

cards.front: How should you use the parking brake after a brake failure?
cards.back: When using the parking brake after a brake failure, hold the release so you can let go if the rear wheels lock, and once stopped, call for help rather than driving on.

cards.front: Why must you never turn the ignition to lock while moving?
cards.back: Never turn the ignition to the lock position while moving in a car with a steering wheel interlock, because the steering will lock and you will lose control.

cards.front: Should you switch off the vehicle while it is moving in a highway emergency?
cards.back: Do not try to switch off the vehicle while it is still moving in a highway emergency.

cards.front: What steps help prevent vehicle theft?
cards.back: To reduce theft, take the keys, lock the doors, never hide a spare key in or near the car, never leave it running unattended, and park in well-lit, patrolled areas.

cards.front: How should you park to help prevent theft?
cards.back: Parking with the front wheels turned sharply right and the emergency brake set helps prevent theft, as can an anti-theft device.

cards.front: What should you do when police signal you to stop?
cards.back: When police signal you to stop, turn on your right turn signal to show you have seen the officer.

cards.front: What might an officer think if you do not signal when being pulled over?
cards.back: If you do not turn on your signal when an officer pulls you over, the officer may think you are avoiding the stop or are impaired.

cards.front: Where should you pull over for police, and what if there is no safe shoulder?
cards.back: Pull over to the right shoulder, never into the center median or the opposite side of a two-lane road, and if there is no safe shoulder slow down with hazards on until you find a safe place.

cards.front: Where should you stop if pulled over at night?
cards.back: If stopped at night, look for a well-lit place such as near street lights, restaurants or service stations, and consider turning on the interior light.

cards.front: What should you do inside the car during a traffic stop?
cards.back: During a traffic stop, stay inside the vehicle unless the officer tells you to get out, end phone calls and turn off the radio.

cards.front: What should you do with tinted windows during a traffic stop?
cards.back: If your windows are tinted, roll them all down after stopping and before the officer reaches you.

cards.front: Where should hands be during a traffic stop, and how do you reach for documents?
cards.back: During a traffic stop, keep hands in view, the driver's on the steering wheel and passengers' on their laps, and tell the officer where documents are before reaching for them.

cards.front: What does signing a traffic ticket mean?
cards.back: Signing a traffic ticket is not an admission of guilt, only an acknowledgment that you received it, and any dispute belongs in traffic court rather than at the roadside.

cards.front: What can happen to a suspected drunk driver who refuses tests?
cards.back: A driver suspected of drunk driving who refuses breath, urine, blood or performance tests can lose driving privileges.

cards.front: What must officers give on request, and where can misconduct be reported?
cards.back: Officers must give their names and badge numbers on request, and misconduct can be reported to their superiors, internal affairs or a civilian complaint board.

cards.front: What are police legally required to do at every traffic stop?
cards.back: Police are legally required to document every traffic stop, including the driver's name and address.

cards.front: When is carbon monoxide most likely to enter a vehicle?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, and it is most likely to enter a vehicle when the heater is on, the exhaust system is faulty, or in heavy traffic.

cards.front: What are the rules for garages and fresh-air vents?
cards.back: Never run a vehicle's engine in a closed garage, and close the fresh-air vent in congested traffic but open it on highways in cold weather.

cards.front: When should the fresh-air vent be closed, and when opened?
cards.back: The fresh-air vent should be closed in congested traffic, yet opened when driving on highways in cold weather.

cards.front: What are symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.back: Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning can include drowsiness or dizziness, bluish skin or lips, headache and increased sensitivity to light.

cards.front: How can you guard against exhaust leaks?
cards.back: A faulty exhaust can leak fumes into the back seat, so have the exhaust checked regularly and listen for any unusual roar under the car.

recap_hooks.text: After a crash, stop, move off the traveled highway unless the crash is serious, and exchange information.
Help the injured as directed and make sure police are notified.
Stop, turn or speed up to avoid a crash, and steer away from oncoming traffic.
If you drift onto the shoulder, ease off and steer back gradually.
In water, do not open the door; unbuckle, open a window, free the children and climb onto the roof.
Alcohol and many drugs impair driving; read medicine labels and ask about side effects.
Weaving, wide turns and driving at night without lights can mean an impaired driver.
In a blowout hold straight and do not brake; when brakes fail, downshift and pump the pedal.
Pull onto the shoulder, turn on hazards and exit on the passenger side.
Signal right, pull onto the right shoulder, stay inside and keep your hands in view.
Signing a ticket only shows you received it.
Carbon monoxide cannot be seen, smelled or tasted, so never run the engine in a closed garage.
